name: Gjalpinulva

related.relation: her mother, by one grandmother's tale (hearsay)
said by superstition to share her fire

facts.text: Gjalpinulva is Midgard's level-80 dragon with 300,000 health. Her lair is in Malmohus (region 100 at 708811, 1021459, which lies in the Malmohus zone); the encounter catalog's label 'Myrkwood' is wrong.

Allakhazam lists Gjalpinulva in Malmohus at level 80; one player wrote that she looks like a dragon with a wolf's head, others that she calls her 'babies' to help her and still talks to those she kills (2006).

She cannot be hurt outside her lair. At every tenth of her health she breathes (Gjalpinulva's Breath) and lowers cold resistance; she glares at one target before a massive attack, stuns everyone near for 30 seconds and throws players.
Waking, her voice booms through the canyons that she is restless and will freeze the flesh and grind the bones of whoever entered her domain.

Her taunts: Odin will do without your aid at Ragnarok; no valkyries will bear you; may your corpse rot on Nastrand; her aunt has a place for you in Niflheim. Over the dead she says their soul now belongs to her.
The script calls her 'she' throughout; bounty text and the 2010s Camelot Herald do too. Allakhazam's patch summary says 'him'. Living Server follows the scripts: she.
Post-period Camelot Herald text says her frozen gaze was sung of in mead halls and that Midgard condemned her; a later chapter says the Varulv were once her allies.
A Dec 2002 Allakhazam comment says fight her inside the lair, and that killing Yar lowers the chance of her exhale (unverified).
Period comments put kills at anywhere from 27 to over 100 players, and a Nov 2003 thread had about 32; Living Server sizes the raid at 70.

Bot chat calls her a daughter of the Fenris wolf (Mythic source not found). In Norse myth Gjalp is a giantess, Geirrod's daughter, whom Thor drove off with a stone; Swedish ulv means wolf (the -ulva ending to verify).
In February 2002 a resist bug let Gjalpinulva be killed in about 30 seconds on the Gawaine server.
Patch 1.100 (2009) let players force her respawn every half hour with Gerrik's Sword; post-period.

In Norse myth the fetter Gleipnir was made of the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath and a bird's spittle; Tyr lost his hand to Fenrir as its pledge.
Nastrand, the shore of corpses, is where oath-breakers and murderers suffer after death in Norse myth.

story:
Midgard's dragon is the Fenris wolf's daughter, the skalds say, born before the gods finished the fetter of six things that do not exist. The accounts of her mother differ: Jordheim names the giantess Gjalp, the grandmothers of Aegir name Iarnvidiur of the Iron Wood, and the svartalfar of Svarhamr say she had none and was breathed out of the frost by her father's last free howl. She flew south over Raumarik and Skona and came down in the nameless ruins of Malmohus, and the cold went out from her like water from a spring. There she drew the frost around her like a cloak, so that outside her court no blow lands, and spread it over the ground of the court itself, so that only there can she bleed.

She bred the drakulv, Yar the firstborn first of all, and ranked them as a court. She called the varulv of Skona to serve her and roared their envoys still for thirty breaths while she named her terms; King Hresvelgr of Varulvhamn refused her, and no werewolf has crossed into Malmohus since. The svartalf miners who came to the ruins met her gaze, and the first of them froze where they stood; the survivors founded the dragonbane of Svarhamr and have watched her ever since.

Midgard's first warband against her, under Hallbjorn of Fort Atla, learned the rules of her court at a terrible price: that she cannot be harmed outside it, that every tenth part of her strength she loses she pays back in a breath of the old winter that strips a fighter's warding against cold, that her stare marks one for death, and that she speaks to the fallen and claims their souls. Its skald Ragnhild lived to tell it. Since then the realm has sent its whole strength south whenever she grows restless and her voice booms through the canyons, and she has always come back, rising again out of the frost of the court, because the chain is not finished. When she dies, a howl crosses Midgard, for her father; the svartalfar say the chain shivers then, and that the day it breaks she will be the first to know.

chapters.title: The Chain of Things That Are Not
chapters.text:
The gods broke two iron chains on the Fenris wolf before the dwarves made Gleipnir, the fetter of six things that do not exist, and Tyr lost his hand to seal it. The skalds of Jordheim add what the gods' version leaves out: finding six things that are not took the dwarves a long time, and in the time between the second chain and the third, the wolf had a daughter.

Who her mother was is the oldest argument in Midgard's dragon lore, and three peoples tell it three ways. The skalds of Jordheim say the giantess Gjalp, daughter of Geirrod, the one who stood astride the river Vimur and made it rise against Thor until he stopped her with a stone; the dragon carries her name, Gjalp, and a she-wolf's ending for her father's line. The grandmothers of Aegir, who live beside the Iarnwood, say the old one Iarnvidiur, who breeds Fenrir's kin in the Iron Wood, and they point to the two-headed wolves of her lair, which have the dragon's look. The svartalfar of Svarhamr, who have watched the dragon longer than anyone, say she had no mother at all: that when the dwarves came with Gleipnir, the wolf howled once, his last free howl, into the frost of the world's edge, and the frost stood up and flew.

All three agree on what she was when she flew. She had her father's head, long and grey, and wings of ice-blue skin, and eyes that froze what they looked at. And she flew south, away from Asgard, while the gods were still congratulating themselves on Tyr's courage and the lightness of the fetter, and none of them looked up.

chapters.title: The Flight South and the Cold Spring
chapters.text:
She flew over Raumarik first. The Galplen folk tell that the wolf, in his youth, had snapped at the sun over that country and spat a splinter of it into the snow, and that his daughter came down there to look at it, and found the dead already gathering around it for warmth, and left them to it; the splinter the Raumarik Revenant keeps is, in their telling, the one thing of her father's she would not take. She crossed Myrkwood and came to Skona Ravine, where the varulv lived, the werewolves who answer to the pack and never to a master, and she rested among them, and they called her kin, because she had a wolf's head.

Then she went on south, past the last farm and the last cairn, to the white broken country at the edge of the world. There were ruins there already: walls and fallen towers of a people nobody in Midgard remembers, older than Jordheim, cut from a grey stone that is not found anywhere else in the realm. The svartalfar say the builders were the first people to see the frost come south, and that they left. The dragon lay down in their ruins, in a hollow among the broken walls on the south-eastern edge, and the cold went out from her like water from a spring. It has not stopped. Malmohus has had no summer since.

Here is where her court was made, and the first rule of it. She drew the frost of the ruins around her like a cloak, the svartalfar say, so close and thick that no blade or spell can pass it; that is why she cannot be hurt when she goes abroad over her land. But in the hollow where she lay down she spread the cloak out on the ground beneath her, as a dog spreads its bedding, and on her own bedding she wears nothing. Only there, in her court, can she bleed. Every raid that has ever fought her has fought her there, and the ones who chased her out of it, thinking her beaten, learned the rule too late.

chapters.title: The Brood
chapters.text:
She was alone in the ruins for a long time, and then she was not. The first of her children was a pup with scales on its back and a wolf's grin, and she licked the frost off it and named it Yar. The svartalfar call him the firstborn, the oldest and strongest of the drakulv and the most powerful of all the werewolves, and he still hunts the south-west of Malmohus with his kin. Whether she bore him or made him out of frost, no one can say; the drakulv do not discuss it.

After Yar came the rest of the drakulv, the dragon-wolves, two-legged and scaled and grinning, and she ranked them as a court is ranked. The missionaries go out to the edges of her land to preach her to whatever will listen. The sacrificers serve her altars, and the soultrappers catch what the sacrificers free. Armguards and axehands and guardians keep her camps; executioners do her justice; disciples study her; protectors stand nearest her court. Above them all are three orders that carry her own magic, whom the svartalfar call by their own names, the klok, the prast and the riddare: the wise ones, the priests and the knights.

Her younger children are dragons. The adolescents of Malmohus, Jarkkonith and Ljoridkorith among them, sun themselves on the ridges and burn whoever comes close; the svartalfar say they are not yet grown, and that it is not known what they will be when they are. The scaled vargs, pups with scales, run in packs through the ruins as hunting dogs.

This is the origin of the second rule of her court. When she is hurt, she calls her babies, and they come out of the ruins at a run: the nearest of her brood, whatever they are, answering their mother. Raids that let them leave the court learned that they do not come back alone. A drakulv who escapes the court returns with others of the camps, and the fight that began with a dragon becomes a fight with Malmohus.

chapters.title: The Werewolves' Refusal
chapters.text:
The varulv of Skona had called her kin. She took them at their word. In the third winter of her court she sent to Skona and to the werewolf haven of Varulvhamn beneath it, where the werewolf nobles gather to talk politics, and summoned their lords to the ruins. They came: the high lords and an old wolfaur of the philosophical kind, and the envoy of King Hresvelgr, who rules the werewolves of Varulvhamn and had taken the name of the eagle-giant whose wings make the wind.

She received them in her court and named her terms. The varulv would serve her as the drakulv served her. They would hunt where she sent them and kill whom she named, and in return they would share in what came when the chain broke. The wolfaur began to answer, and she roared. It was the first time anyone outside her brood had heard it: a roar that held every werewolf in the court motionless, unable to lift a paw, for as long as a man can hold his breath, while she repeated her terms slowly into their faces. That is the third rule of her court, the long stun that falls on everyone near her. Raids still break out of it the way the werewolves did, one at a time, and late.

The envoy carried her terms home. King Hresvelgr heard them in his hall and gave his answer in the werewolves' one law: a wolf answers to the pack and never to a master, and a pack that kills because it is told to has a master. The varulv withdrew from Malmohus. None of them has set foot in it since, and Skona's werewolves stand at the edge of the ravine and look south and do not go further. The heralds of a later age wrote that the varulv were once her allies. The werewolves do not deny it. They say they were allies, once, and then they were asked to be servants, and that is a different thing.

chapters.title: The Frozen Svartalfar
chapters.text:
The svartalfar came to Malmohus for the grey stone. A clan of dark elves from under Myrkwood heard that the ruins at the edge of the world were cut from a stone found nowhere else, and that it rang like a bell when struck and held enchantments better than iron, and they came south with picks to mine the fallen towers. They knew there was a dragon. They thought the ruins were large enough to share.

Their foreman, a svartalf the clan remembers as Sviga, went to look at her, because a foreman should know what he is working beside. He came to the edge of the hollow and she looked at him. The clan found him there the next morning, still standing, still looking, frozen through, with frost on his open eyes. Others went to bring him back, and she looked at them too. The frozen svartalfar still stand in the ruins of Malmohus, and the bestiaries of Midgard list them with the living, because they have never fallen down.

That is the gaze the mead halls sang of in a later age, and the origin of the fourth rule of her court: when she fixes one fighter with her stare, the next thing she does kills what she is staring at. The svartalfar call it her glare. A fighter who sees her eyes on him runs, and keeps running until she looks away.

The clan did not go home. They built the town of Svarhamr at the edge of her land, at a distance they measured by the frozen ones, and they swore that they would see her dead. They are the dragonbane svartalfar, and they have watched her ever since, the way fishermen watch weather. They count her wakings and her sleeps. They pay any friend of theirs to kill her firstborn, because a dragon in grief breathes less carefully. Kiaja keeps their trust, and Raxnathor their rewards. Every child of Svarhamr is taken once to see the frozen foreman, and told his name.

chapters.title: Hallbjorn's Warband
chapters.text:
In the years of the war between the realms, when Midgard's frontier was keeps and banners, the realm sent its first warband south to kill her. It mustered at Fort Atla in Gotar under Hallbjorn Ulfsson, a thane who had held Glenlock against Albion, and it was eighty strong, and it had a skald with it, Ragnhild of Galplen, to sing the victory. Ragnhild lived. Most of the eighty did not. Her song of the warband is the oldest account of the dragon's court, and every warband since has learned the rules of her court from it.

Hallbjorn found her abroad over the ruins and attacked her there, and the warband's blows slid off the frost-cloak like rain off a roof, and she laughed and went back to her hollow. They followed her in. In the court their blades bit, and the warband cheered, and then she paid them back. Every time they took a tenth part of her strength, she drew breath and breathed out a tenth part of the old winter she carries, and it washed over the whole court. The breath did not only freeze; it stripped away whatever warding against cold a fighter had brought, so that the next breath bit deeper. That is the fifth rule: the breath at every tenth, and the cold that eats your defences. Ragnhild counted nine breaths in her song. The warband did not hear the ninth. Hallbjorn himself reached her flank, and she caught him with a sweep of her body and flung him across the court like a sack, which is the sixth rule: whoever is underfoot does not stay there.

The skald lay among the dead at the end, unhurt but frozen to the ground, and heard the dragon speak to them. Your soul belongs to me now, she told each one, by craft, as if she knew them: the thane, the healer, the runemaster. She told them Odin would do without them at Ragnarok and that no valkyries would carry them, and that her aunt kept a place for them in Niflheim. Ragnhild understood that the aunt was Hel. When the dragon flew, the skald crawled out of the court and walked home to Fort Atla, and sang. The raids of every age since have reported the same thing: she talks to the dead. The wise ones release quickly.

chapters.title: The Restless Wakings
chapters.text:
She does not die and stay dead. When a raid kills her, a howl crosses all of Midgard, from Malmohus to Odin's Gate, a soul-piercing sound that every farmer in Gotar has heard at least once and then all is quiet. In a season, or less, she is in her court again. The svartalfar say she rises out of the frost of the hollow, because the cloak she spread there remembers her shape; the skalds say a daughter of the wolf cannot finish dying while her father's chain is not finished either. Either way, the realm's dragonslayers are never out of work.

Between raids she sleeps, and when she wakes she is restless. Her voice booms through the canyons of Malmohus, asking who has dared to enter her domain and promising to freeze their flesh and grind their bones to dust, and the drakulv in every camp lift their heads. Svarhamr keeps a tally of her wakings carved on a beam of the meeting hall. The dragonbane learned long ago to wake her when it suited them; a later age of the heralds recorded a blade, Gerrik's Sword, that could call her up out of the frost on purpose, and the svartalfar say there were other ways before that one, which they do not share.

Once, the heralds recorded, her breath failed her. It was the winter after the realms' first raids, and a warband on one of the far shores of the realm found her weak, her winter not answering, and killed her in the time it takes to say a prayer. The skalds made a drinking song of it. The svartalfar made a note on their beam. The next winter her breath was back, and the skalds stopped singing the song.

The beam in Svarhamr records every warband that came after Hallbjorn's. A hundred came from Jordheim in one restless year and died inside the hollow without wounding her past the second breath. Another warband, from the keeps of Uppland, lasted as long as a skald takes to sing one verse. A small company of twenty-seven out of Galplen, who had read Ragnhild's song until they knew it by heart, killed her twice in one day and went home with two scales. The dragonbane carved their names deepest. And one belief came south from Odin's Gate with the frontier warbands: that the Glacier Giant on the frontier shares her fire, and that killing him first leaves her breath weaker. The svartalfar have never seen any sign of it on their beam. The warbands kill the giant anyway.

chapters.title: What She Waits For
chapters.text:
The old songs say that at the end the wolf will break free. Gleipnir will part, Fenrir will run with his jaws so wide that the lower one scrapes the earth and the upper one the sky, and he will swallow Odin. The ship of nails will sail from the north. The dead of Nastrand, the shore of corpses where oath-breakers lie, will rise. And Hel will come with her host out of Niflheim.

Gjalpinulva knows all this. She is the only one of the three realms' dragons who speaks of the end, and she speaks of it as a promise. When she tells a warrior that Odin will have to do without his aid at Ragnarok, she means it as a fact about the coming battle: the warrior will be in Niflheim with her aunt, and the gods will be one spear short. Every soul she claims in her court is one fewer for the valkyries to carry to Valhalla, and one more for the host that comes out of the north at the end.

The svartalfar of Svarhamr believe she is waiting for the chain to break, and that while she lives Gleipnir is not finished, because she was born in the time before the last of its six things was found. That is why some of them hope for her death, and why some of them, quietly, fear it: if her death finishes the chain, it may also start the end. The skalds of Jordheim believe she is waiting for her father, and that the day he runs she will fly north to meet him with her brood behind her, Yar at the front and her adolescent dragons grown at last. The grandmothers of Aegir believe nothing so grand. They say she is a daughter waiting for her father to come home, and that there is no creature more dangerous.

Some in Midgard look at the dead dragon under Tuscaran Glacier, the one the rime giants built on, and wonder whether the end was tried once before and failed. Gjalpinulva has never said. When she dies, she howls for her father, and the svartalfar say that somewhere under the earth the chain shivers. When it breaks, they say, she will be the first to know. Midgard intends to keep killing her until then.

legend: Fight her in the lair, never outside: out there she can't be hurt and she knows it, and a Dec 2002 comment warned that attacks from outside trigger her area breath anyway. Cold resists up and keep them up, because every breath at each 10% strips them; healers re-buff after each one. When she stares at someone, that someone runs out of the glare. Stun breaks for the long roar, which lasts thirty seconds. Kill her babies before they reach the healers, and don't let the brood leave the lair, because they come back with friends. Period kills ran from 27 people to over 100; a 74-strong raid once lasted three minutes. Old raiders swore that killing Yar first made her breathe less; the heralds never said so, but people still do it. Never say her name inside the ruins.

I grow restless. Who dares my domain? I will grind your bones to dust!

phases.text: Breathe in, little ones. It is the last cold air you will taste.
My father broke a god's hand. What do you think I will break?
I grow restless. Who has dared to enter my domain?
Father! The chain! Do you feel it shiver?

loremasterTopic.text: Fenris's daughter, the skalds say, with a wolf's head, wings and a frozen gaze. She calls Niflheim's keeper her aunt and promises the dead no valkyries. Out of her lair she cannot be wounded. In it she breathes winter at every tenth of her strength and calls her brood, the drakulv, to her side.

bookPage: Sung at the hall of Svarhamr, as the dragonbane svartalfar sing it, which is not how Jordheim sings it. The wolf was bound with a chain of things that are not. Before the last link closed he had a daughter, and she flew south while the gods were busy congratulating themselves. She came down in Malmohus among the ruins of a people nobody remembers, and she lay down there, and the frost went out from her like water from a spring. The svartalfar have watched her ever since. They say she is waiting for the chain to break. They say when it does, she will be the first to know. They say that is why they watch.
